# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in Rules.

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in Input. The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in Controls.

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in Visuals. The game stays silent as defined in Sound.

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in Reproducibility. Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in Technology. Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in Architecture.

Use the journeys in Acceptance to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in Input, which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as Input describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

## Documentation map

Every project document, by area. Project-wide policies apply to all new work, including work that doesn't mention them.

### Gameplay

- rules.md: Card matching, moves, timing and victory rules
- deck-generation.md: Board-code parsing, paired deck construction, deterministic shuffle arithmetic, and fresh seed selection.
- selection-state.md: The closed, one-card, and mismatch selection alternatives, visibility, and decoding boundaries.
- turn-resolution.md: Activation guards, second-reveal resolution, and the ordering of time, feedback, and turns.
- scoring-and-moves.md: Pair progress, move accounting, minimum completions, and continued play at the move cap.
- best-score-records.md: Per-size best move comparison, preference validation, persistence, and imported-completion behavior.
- board-size-catalogue.md: The seven board sizes, exact card and pair counts, included faces, and size selection behavior.
- win-conditions.md: Full matched coverage, the final transition, stopped time, and played versus imported completion.
- game-state-model.md: GameState fields, invariants, derived values, immutable transitions, and session boundaries.
- pair-identity.md: Position indices versus face numbers, artwork identity dimensions, and hidden-face rendering.
- mismatch-interval.md: The exact 800-millisecond active interval, synchronization, pauses, and stale timer protection.
- elapsed-time-rules.md: Active-time accumulation, browser observations, display conversion, caps, and snapshot precision.
- new-game-and-restart.md: What fresh deals, repeats, size changes, loads, Resume, exports, and reloads preserve or reset.
- gameplay-faq.md: Answers to common play and maintenance questions, with links to detailed behavior pages.

### Controls and input

- controls.md: Game options and reproduction controls
- input.md: Pointer, touch, keyboard and focus behavior
- control-bar.md: The deal buttons, size selector, responsive arrangement and session callbacks in Controls.tsx.
- reproduction-panel.md: Board-code drafts, snapshot editing, load outcomes, export and Resume behavior.
- status-bar.md: The statistics definition list, counter sources, elapsed display and completion output.
- board-keyboard-navigation.md: Arrow target calculations, remembered board entry, DOM focus and nearest scrolling.
- pointer-and-touch.md: Native click and tap activation, press timing and scrolling through large boards.
- focus-policy.md: Current action focus and board memory, plus the policy for main-screen replacements.
- dialog-policy.md: The leave-work confirmation policy and its boundary with current direct deal actions.
- target-size-policy.md: The new-control size policy, existing CSS dimensions and rendered target measurement.
- text-entry-policy.md: Accepted name representation and its separation from board-code and JSON input.
- name-length-policy.md: Name-length acceptance, Unicode counting units and boundary examples.
- duplicate-names-policy.md: Group-scoped name comparison, case handling and evidence for repeat detection.
- announcements-policy.md: Status publication, repeated event identity, turn results and load feedback.
- tables-policy.md: The result-table markup policy and how it differs from current statistics and cards.
- screen-reader-notes.md: A complete game through exposed names and states, with accessibility evidence limits.
- form-layout-guide.md: Label associations, responsive field rows, text editing surfaces and load-notice layout.
- error-display-guide.md: Load validation, visible notices, preserved drafts, focus and retry behavior.
- native-controls-guide.md: Native element choices and the browser behavior retained around React callbacks.
- disabled-state-guide.md: Matched ARIA state, game eligibility, imported pause and continued focus movement.
- interface-review-checklist.md: Populated interface review journeys and the source or browser evidence for each.

### Visuals

- visuals.md: Layout, card artwork, colors and motion
- motion-policy.md: Current card and completion effects, reduced motion, session flags and motion test coverage.
- color-policy.md: Interface and artwork color roles, redundant state cues, palette indexing and color checks.
- card-artwork.md: Card props, hidden-face rendering, button naming, back decoration, face SVG and matched overlays.
- face-catalogue.md: All face identity ranges, shape paths, marker coordinates, fill modes and face-sheet evidence.
- layout-grid.md: Page and board sizing, width calculations, scrollbars, responsive wrapping and layout tests.
- zoom-behaviour.md: Equivalent zoom geometry, text reflow, native controls and playable scrolling boards.
- theme-tokens.md: Existing CSS variables, literal values, artwork color tables and their cascade relationships.
- spacing-scale.md: Authored spacing values by component, resets, scroll clearance and the computed spacing audit.
- typography.md: System font inheritance, text hierarchy, numeric styling, controls and text readability evidence.
- large-board-rendering.md: Full 256-card rendering, bounded scrolling, focus clearance, touch input and rendering optimizations.
- icon-and-glyph-policy.md: Why the current artwork uses SVG paths and CSS decoration, with native control affordances.
- contrast-audit.md: Reproducible sRGB contrast calculations for surfaces, text, artwork and the pulse midpoint.
- visual-review-checklist.md: Existing visual requirements and relevant source tests grouped into a concrete review journey.

### Sound

- sound.md: Game sound behavior
- feedback-without-audio.md: Traces silent card, turn, status, completion and load feedback through the current components and checks.
- audio-research-notes.md: Records the discarded audio exploration and relates its tradeoffs to the current silent design and evidence.

### Sharing and formats

- reproducibility.md: Board codes, snapshots and replay formats
- data-exchange-policy.md: How board codes, snapshots and replays cross application boundaries, with policy for future exports.
- import-safety-policy.md: Untrusted-input validation, replacement safety, current diagnostics and the field-error policy.
- board-code-format.md: Version 1 code syntax, exact deal generation, bounded draws and independent vectors.
- snapshot-format.md: Snapshot fields, shared JSON helpers, consistency checks, rounding and import lifecycle.
- replay-format.md: Replay schema, logical timing, validation results and CLI conversion to a final snapshot.
- snapshot-selection-notes.md: How matched positions and selection variants are validated against a regenerated deck.
- format-versioning-guide.md: Format and product versions, exact-key compatibility and changes to artifact meaning.
- sharing-faq.md: Practical answers for copying deals, loading progress, fixing drafts and reporting sharing bugs.

### Persistence

- persistence-overview.md: What the current game saves, what remains in memory and which persistence page to consult.
- persistence-envelope.md: The feature JSON envelope and its distinction from the existing versioned preference aggregate.
- retention-policy.md: Saved-list retention, aggregate best-score lifetime and the absence of an attempt history.
- storage-failure-policy.md: Unavailable-storage behavior, feature feedback and the current adapter’s catch boundaries.
- corrupt-data-policy.md: Preference validation, silent rejection and the timing of read rejection and later replacement.
- preferences-store.md: Code-level guide to preference data, best selection, browser-store acquisition and the save effect.
- storage-quota-notes.md: Measured preference payload sizes, browser capacity guidance and the scope of quota evidence.
- private-browsing-notes.md: Private-session storage lifetime, denied operations and comparisons that distinguish their effects.
- storage-testing-guide.md: Existing persistence tests and practical checks for decoding, failures, completion and reload.

### Competition

- competition-overview.md: Purpose and social context of shared-device competition, with an honest boundary around the solo implementation.
- competition-pairing.md: Entry-order seeds and opening pairings for four- and eight-person brackets, with named examples.
- competition-rounds.md: Round names and their displayed text, with distinctions between event stages and browser session generations.
- competition-boards.md: Board dimensions by stage, their face sets, and implications for layout and navigation.
- competition-deals.md: Match deal identity, board-code reproducibility, and the limits of the current fresh-deal helper.
- competition-ties.md: Ordered result comparison, active-time precision, and seed priority for equal results.
- competition-scores.md: Competition isolation from ordinary saved size and best moves, including the current session write paths.
- competition-research.md: Playtests about face recognition, keyboard travel, device handoff and spectating.

### Architecture and technology

- architecture.md: Game code structure and module responsibilities
- technology.md: Language, package versions, build and distribution
- module-layout-policy.md: Behavior ownership, dependency direction and feature placement in the game source.
- dependency-policy.md: Locked packages, runtime versus tooling roles and dependency evidence.
- randomness-policy.md: Fresh seed selection, rejection sampling and the boundary with reproducible decks.
- time-policy.md: Active-time ownership, pause conditions, synchronization and logical interval handling.
- test-policy.md: Unit, source and browser verification layers and what their results establish.
- source-layout.md: A file-by-file map of application code, tooling, diagnostics and test support.
- session-module.md: Session fields, controller actions, replacement generations and preference effects.
- react-boundaries.md: React components, hooks, local state and the data-only rule boundary.
- build-pipeline.md: Manifest commands, compiler checks, Vite entries and production versus diagnostic output.
- offline-delivery.md: Single-file distribution, disk and HTTP behavior and self-containment evidence.
- clock-design.md: Clock arithmetic, timeout scheduling, visibility ordering and stale-work cleanup.
- purity-guide.md: Explicit inputs, immutable transitions, validation and effect separation in the core.
- typescript-settings.md: Compiler projects, exact options, strictness and environment coverage.
- css-organization.md: Stylesheet ownership, global cascade, grid geometry and visual-test seams.
- source-audit-notes.md: Source inspection patterns, discovery, package checks and regex coverage limits.
- code-review-guide.md: Behavior-focused review paths and evidence for rules, lifecycle, formats and delivery.

### Decisions

- adr-001-react.md: This record explains why React owns the browser view while plain functions own the game rules.
- adr-002-typescript.md: This record explains the strict TypeScript model and why parsed data still needs runtime validation.
- adr-003-single-file.md: This record explains the single HTML distribution and the distinction between delivery and source organization.
- adr-004-no-backend.md: This record explains why the playable game has no backend and what that means for records and sharing.
- adr-005-vite.md: This record explains Vite’s role in transforming the source and producing the offline artifact.
- adr-006-native-controls.md: This record explains why cards and controls use browser elements rather than custom interaction widgets.
- adr-007-svg-faces.md: This record explains the generated SVG artwork and why face identity is expressed through geometry.
- adr-008-seven-sizes.md: This record explains the supported board sizes and their effect on rules, artwork and layout.

- adr-012-no-sound.md: This record explains why Neon Pairs uses visual state and accessible text feedback without game audio.
- adr-013-monotonic-clock.md: This record explains measured browser deltas, fractional milliseconds and the separation from logical game time.
- adr-014-pause-on-hidden.md: This record explains why hiding the page suspends both elapsed time and a pending mismatch interval.
- adr-015-replay-cli.md: This record explains why replay is a command-line diagnostic and how it shares the browser’s rules.
- adr-016-no-state-library.md: This record explains why the game uses React state and explicit transitions without a global state library.
- adr-017-colocated-tests.md: This record explains the split between neighboring unit tests and application-level browser journeys.

- adr-023-results-as-lists.md: This historical record explains the retired ordered-list presentation for rankings and results.

- adr-039-contrast-floor.md: This record explains the contrast rationale and the limits of the palette and artwork evidence.
- adr-040-file-size-aim.md: This record explains the compact-artifact aim and its architectural tradeoffs.
- adr-041-name-limits.md: This historical record explains the retired one-to-thirty-two-character name limit and literal storage choice.
- adr-042-error-copy.md: This record explains the current reproduction errors and why failed validation leaves the game available.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in Rules:

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow Input and Controls. Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against Visuals. Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking Sound. Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check Reproducibility with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in Technology. Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against Architecture.

# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the reproducibility formats.

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. Input defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The game specification defines the behavior this structure implements.
# ADR 003: Distribute one HTML file

This record explains the single HTML distribution and the distinction between delivery and source organization.

## Context

A player should be able to save the game, open it later and still have the complete board, artwork and controls. A directory full of scripts, images and fonts creates several opportunities for a copied game to become incomplete. Moving just the HTML can lose a stylesheet; a remote font or sprite can stop loading away from the network. The original distribution discussion therefore focused on what a player actually receives.

The chosen artifact is `dist/index.html`. It contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play and can open directly from disk. The source remains a set of focused TypeScript, TSX and CSS files. Single-file delivery was never an argument for putting the whole implementation into one authored module. Source layout documents the source arrangement.

## Build decision

Vite combines React transformation with `vite-plugin-singlefile`. The main configuration sets the target to `es2023` and disables module preload. A preload helper would have no useful chunks to fetch in the final inline page. The source comment records that reason, and `build-output.e2e.test.ts` inspects the HTML for the unwanted fetch and preload code.

The source `index.html` is an entry document containing a root element and a module reference to `src/main.tsx`. It is not itself the final self-contained game. Copying it before a build would preserve a development entry path rather than deliver the playable artifact. This distinction matters when reporting that an offline test passed.

## What the choice buys

An offline copy is straightforward to archive and pass between machines. Inline SVG faces need no image directory. The system font needs no font request. There is no runtime account or service configuration to carry alongside the file. These choices reinforce the artifact boundary; see ADR 004, ADR 007 and ADR 027.

Browser tests cover the built artifact, including opening from a file URL with network access blocked. This is more informative than observing that a development server happened to have everything cached. The browser test command builds current source before running, so its distribution evidence refers to the current implementation.

## Tradeoffs

A single HTML file gives up separate long-lived asset caches. An update replaces the complete artifact rather than just a changed script. For a small game with generated artwork and no remote resources, that cost was accepted in exchange for reliable copying and local opening. The bundle is still a real bundle, so package size and build output remain relevant; ADR 040 discusses the compact-artifact aim.

Saved preferences are a separate concern. Storage behavior for file URLs varies between browsers. The project uses a local HTTP origin when checking persistence, while direct disk opening checks that the game plays. A usable offline artifact does not promise that every browser treats its file storage like a stable web origin.

The diagnostic face sheet and session harness also have single-file builds, but they are separate outputs under `.art` and `.session`. They are not extra files a player needs, and they are not embedded debugging routes inside the shipped page. ADR 051 explains why that separation is useful.

## The distribution configuration

The same configuration used by the build keeps development watcher exclusions separate from the offline output settings.

```ts
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import { viteSingleFile } from 'vite-plugin-singlefile';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), viteSingleFile()],
  // One inline file has no chunks to preload, so leave out the preload helper and its fetch call.
  build: { target: 'es2023', modulePreload: false },
  server: {
    watch: {
      ignored: ['**/.browser-work/**', '**/.playwright-browsers/**', '**/.npm-cache/**'],
    },
  },
});
```
# ADR 004: Keep play local

This record explains why the playable game has no backend and what that means for records and sharing.

## Decision

Neon Pairs runs its game rules in the browser and needs no application server. There is no account, API key or remote score service. A local development server and the HTTP server used in tests serve files; neither is a gameplay backend. The distinction is practical: opening the built HTML from disk still provides the game.

A memory game needs a deck, a turn state, a clock and a way to display progress. All four can live locally. Adding a backend would create deployment, connectivity and identity questions without improving the required action of revealing and matching cards. The accepted scope therefore uses local preferences for size and best moves and explicit text formats for reproducing a game.

## How information moves

`freshBoardCode` chooses a browser seed. `createGame` reconstructs the deck from the code. `activateCard` and `advanceGame` update the data. The session adapter owns browser time and preference writes. None of those operations needs a request to another process.

A board code can be copied to repeat a starting arrangement. A snapshot can be exported into a textarea and copied manually to preserve progress. Replay files support engineering investigations through the CLI. Those mechanisms supply useful sharing without a hosted document store. They also make the limits clear: a board code has no progress, and local JSON validation establishes structural consistency rather than verified provenance. See Sharing FAQ and Reproducibility.

## Records are local evidence

`Preferences` contains a selected size and a map of best move counts. `rememberBest` compares a completed result with the entry for that size. This is a convenience for one browser's player, not an authority about play on other machines. The storage parser checks supported sizes and plausible bounded integer scores; it does not authenticate the person who produced them.

That limitation was acceptable because the product does not depend on trusted remote standings. Treating local data as untrusted also helps ordinary reliability. A malformed preference value falls back to usable defaults instead of preventing a deal. An unavailable storage object leaves the current game playable. Persistence overview describes the operational detail.

## Alternatives considered

A thin score service looked superficially small, but it would have needed a definition of identity, abuse handling and trustworthy results. Merely accepting a move count posted by a browser would add networking without adding integrity. A server-generated deck would also complicate opening the game offline and reproducing a deal outside the UI.

A hosted-only static site would avoid backend logic but still make the launch path depend on a reachable origin. The chosen build can be hosted as a file and can also be retained locally. Hosting is a distribution option, not a prerequisite embedded in the rules.

## Consequences for engineering

Debugging relies on documented board codes, snapshots, replay actions and browser artifacts. It does not rely on inspecting a server session. The pure game functions make that a strength: a reported action sequence can run in Node with the same matching behavior. ADR 015 records that diagnostic path.

There is no remote recovery promise for an unexported in-memory game. A page reload starts a fresh deal, using a saved supported size when one is available. This follows the current session model rather than attempting to infer a cloud-save feature from local preferences. The absence of a backend also informs ADR 038, but that decision has its own reasons about what the game observes.

## Local preference data

The stored model is deliberately small. The adapter interface permits failure tests without turning the game core into a storage client.

```ts
export const DEFAULT_SIZE = GRID_SIZES[0];
export const PREFERENCES_KEY = 'neon-pairs.preferences.v1';
export const PREFERENCES_VERSION = 1;
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
export interface PreferenceStore {
  getItem(key: string): string | null;
  setItem(key: string, value: string): void;
}
```
# ADR 010: Save progress as explicit JSON

This record explains the JSON snapshot format, its validation boundary and its relationship to a board code.

## Decision

Export progress as readable version 1 JSON. The snapshot contains `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. It derives the deck from the code and derives completion from matched positions. There is no second serialized deck, pair total or win flag to reconcile with the underlying data.

JSON was selected because both browser and Node tools can read it, a person can inspect it during a bug report, and copying it from a textarea needs no additional file or clipboard API. The export uses two-space indentation. Formatting makes a report easier to read, while validation relies on values rather than indentation.

## Coherent state, not arbitrary fields

`decodeSnapshot` treats parsed data as unknown. It checks the complete shape, version, code, bounded integer counters, matched positions and selection. Extra keys are rejected. Matched positions must be unique, in range and form whole face pairs. A pending mismatch needs two different unmatched positions whose faces differ, with remaining time from 1 through 800 whole milliseconds.

The decoder also checks relationships. Moves must cover the matched pairs and a pending mismatch. An unstarted game has no progress. A started game with zero moves needs its first revealed card. These checks prevent combinations that contradict the current state rules without requiring an exhaustive reconstruction of earlier play. Snapshot selection notes explains the selection cases.

## Representation details

Positions are zero-based row-order indices. Export sorts matched positions so equivalent sets have a stable readable ordering. Active time can retain fractions in memory; export floors elapsed milliseconds and rounds pending mismatch time upward. Rounding the remaining interval upward keeps a still-open mismatch from becoming a zero-duration serialized state.

The UTF-8 snapshot limit is 65536 bytes. The textarea also has a character limit, but the parser's byte check is the format boundary. This matters because a character count and a UTF-8 byte count are not interchangeable in general. `TextEncoder` supplies the byte measurement in the shared format helper.

## Import as a session action

Validation completes before the controller replaces the current game. Invalid text leaves the active game and draft available. Valid unfinished progress enters a paused session until Resume. That gives the player time to inspect what loaded instead of consuming a short remaining mismatch interval during the act of importing. Completed progress follows its completed presentation path. ADR 037 explains the pause choice.

Snapshot state does not include the board's remembered focus, the open state of the reproduction disclosure or a textarea draft. Those are presentation concerns. The reconstructed board starts with its ordinary focus memory, and the session controls retain their documented focus behavior.

## Alternatives and consequences

Serializing the entire internal session object would have exported browser bookkeeping such as the generation counter and announcement sequence. It would also have made implementation refactors into accidental format changes. Saving only a board code would have been smaller but could not preserve moves or a half-finished turn.

A binary format could reduce size at the expense of inspectability and implementation complexity. For this bounded state, explicit JSON is already compact enough and easier to diagnose. The shared encoder is also the replay CLI's output, giving that tool a familiar final-state format. See Snapshot format, ADR 048 and Data exchange policy.

## The exported representation

The encoder names its public fields explicitly instead of stringifying the entire GameState object.

```ts
export const SNAPSHOT_VERSION = 1;
export const SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES = 65_536;
export const SNAPSHOT_KEYS = [
  'version',
  'boardCode',
  'matched',
  'selection',
  'moves',
  'elapsedMs',
  'started',
] as const;

export function encodeSnapshot(state: GameState): string {
  return JSON.stringify(
    {
      version: SNAPSHOT_VERSION,
      boardCode: state.boardCode,
      matched: [...state.matched].sort((left, right) => left - right),
      // Active time keeps its fractions in play. Export writes whole milliseconds, and rounding
      // pending time up keeps a mismatch at 1ms or more.
      selection:
        state.selection.kind === SelectionKind.mismatch
          ? { ...state.selection, remainingMs: Math.ceil(state.selection.remainingMs) }
          : state.selection,
      moves: state.moves,
      elapsedMs: Math.floor(state.elapsedMs),
      started: state.started,
    },
    null,
    2,
  );
}
```
# ADR 011: Version local keys by data family

This historical record explains the original dotted storage keys and the reasoning behind the preferences key.

Status: Superseded by ADR 058: storage namespace

## Original setting

The first persistent data was small: a chosen grid size and local best move counts. It lived beside other applications on a browser origin, so a generic key such as `settings` would have been easy to collide with. The storage discussion treated key naming as a way to identify ownership and make saved data recognizable during debugging.

The decision at that time was that stored data uses keys of the form `neon-pairs.THING.v1`. The prefix identified the game, the middle segment identified the data family and the suffix identified the stored format generation. The existing preferences key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, follows that decision. Its name was intended to be understandable in browser storage tools without requiring a separate registry.

## Why that structure seemed sufficient

Combining size and best moves in one preferences value made the initial storage surface easy to inspect. A reload could read one JSON document and either accept its supported values or return a default size with no best records. The document also carried `schemaVersion: 1`, so the reader could check the structure after locating the key.

The duplication between a versioned key and a version field was deliberate. The key selected a family of stored data; the field protected the parser from an unrelated or damaged value placed there. A recognizable name did not establish that the JSON was valid. Preferences store describes the actual parser.

## Alternatives considered at the time

One unqualified key for the whole application would have been shorter. It would also have hidden ownership and made unrelated applications sharing an origin more likely to reuse the name. A separate key for each score would have made individual entries easy to inspect but spread validation and writes over several values.

The chosen envelope kept the selected size and all per-size bests together. It did not store active progress. That distinction kept routine preference writes from becoming an implicit saved-game mechanism. Exported snapshots already had their own explicit representation and did not need to be mixed into settings merely because they were JSON.

## Failure behavior was part of the reasoning

The storage adapter exposed `getItem` and `setItem`, allowing a fake store to throw during tests. Parsing, access and writing could all fail without preventing the in-memory game from proceeding. Reading a versioned key therefore did not imply that persistence was always available. The browser origin still controlled access, and direct disk opening had browser-dependent storage behavior.

The reader checked the saved side length against the supported catalogue and checked score entries against the move limits. A key name was not used as a substitute for these checks. Similarly, ownership of one key gave no reason to clear other origin data when a value was rejected.

## Historical consequence

This record explains why a dotted versioned preferences key exists in the current source. It is not the naming authority for additional stored families. The replacement decision is ADR 058; it addresses new names without requiring the current preferences value to be renamed.

That distinction prevents a maintenance error in which a developer reads an old record, treats its original rationale as current policy and spreads the retired naming scheme. It also preserves the useful part of the history: the preferences name was a considered design choice, not an arbitrary leftover. Persistence envelope covers the current value and Corrupt data policy covers rejection behavior.

## The surviving preferences identifier

This is present-day evidence of the original decision’s effect. It is not evidence that every future data family follows the old scheme.

```ts
export const DEFAULT_SIZE = GRID_SIZES[0];
export const PREFERENCES_KEY = 'neon-pairs.preferences.v1';
export const PREFERENCES_VERSION = 1;
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
export interface PreferenceStore {
  getItem(key: string): string | null;
  setItem(key: string, value: string): void;
}
```
# ADR 023: Present rankings as ordered lists

This historical record explains the retired ordered-list presentation for rankings and results.

Status: Superseded by Tables policy

## Original context

The early results sketch emphasized a phone-sized page. A sequence of entries could be stacked vertically, with the name and result together and little need for horizontal movement. At that point, the team chose ordered lists for rankings and results because they read well on phones.

This was a presentation decision in the original design discussion; the current game has no ranking screen. The current playable implementation shows its own move count, pair progress, time and per-size best.

## Decision as made

Each entry would have been one list row, with ordering carrying the ranking meaning. Supporting text could sit under the primary name without creating a wide grid. The list's native numbering appeared to provide a useful relationship between visual position and reading order.

The design favored following one entry from top to bottom over scanning one metric down a column. That was a reasonable priority while the imagined result was a short linear reading task. It also made the narrow-screen prototype straightforward to build using familiar block layout.

## Reasons that supported the choice

An ordered list can express a sequence without an additional position field in every visible row. It adapts naturally to wrapping text, and native list semantics are familiar to accessibility tools. With few fields, a list gives each entry enough vertical space without forcing a compact row height.

The team also wanted to avoid a horizontal scrolling area outside the game board. A stacked entry appeared to solve that on small screens and kept the imagined results section visually close to ordinary prose. The old decision therefore came from a concrete reading concern, not from treating a list as a universally better data structure.

## Alternatives discussed

A tabular layout was more structured and better suited to comparisons across repeated fields. In the earliest sketch, that benefit seemed less urgent than fitting an entire entry into a phone width. Cards for individual results were another option, but they would have added visual framing while leaving the same question of how to compare one field across entries.

Plain paragraphs were rejected as too weak a representation of order. A manually typed rank inside every paragraph would have reproduced part of an ordered list without its structural meaning. The initial list choice was therefore internally coherent for the information the sketch expected to emphasize.

## Why this is historical

The weakness of a stacked list becomes apparent when readers want to compare the same metric across several entries. Repeated labels take space, and values no longer align in a way that supports scanning. The original rationale optimized the reading of an individual result and gave less weight to cross-entry relationships.

Tables policy is the replacement decision. The relevant historical lesson is that narrow-screen layout alone was too small a basis for choosing a representation of comparative data. The information's relationships also matter.

## Connection to the current code

`GameStatus.tsx` uses a definition list for the current game's labeled statistics and a paragraph for completion. That is a different information shape from a ranked collection of participants. It should not be interpreted as an implementation of this old ordered-list decision or as evidence against the replacement page.

Status bar, Tables policy and Interface review checklist are useful companions when reviewing actual screens. The superseding link at the top is the authority boundary: this historical rationale can explain a prototype, but it does not direct a new results presentation.
# ADR 041: Allow short names as typed

This historical record explains the retired one-to-thirty-two-character name limit and literal storage choice.

Status: Superseded by Name length policy

## Original context

The early name-entry discussion favored a small amount of validation. Names were expected to be short labels, not account identities, and the team wanted to avoid transforming a person's text unexpectedly. The initial rule allowed names with 1 to 32 characters and stored them exactly as typed.

That choice belonged to an earlier interface design discussion. The game has no player-name entry field in its current control tree. Its text fields are a board code and snapshot JSON, with format-specific limits.

## Decision as originally made

The lower limit excluded an empty label. The upper limit was intended to keep an entry reasonably compact on a phone while allowing more than a very short nickname. Saving the original text was meant to preserve capitalization, spacing choices and the visible spelling a person had entered.

The team treated name validation as a presentation concern rather than an identity-verification system. No account lookup or remote uniqueness check was involved. That matched the broader local-game approach: a label helped readers recognize an entry, but did not establish a trusted person behind a result.

## Reasoning

Transforming text can surprise people when the displayed result differs from the field they submitted. Literal storage looked easy to explain and easy to debug: the saved value would match the original draft. A modest length range appeared sufficient for a prototype with only a few entries.

A larger range would have made wrapping and compact layouts harder to assess. A much smaller range risked excluding ordinary names without a clear gameplay reason. The original 32-character ceiling was a pragmatic visual estimate, not a result derived from the deck or scoring model.

## Alternatives considered then

Fixed abbreviations would have kept rows compact but shifted the burden to users to shorten their own labels. Automatically truncating would have silently changed identity cues. Rejecting a long draft was considered clearer than saving a shortened version that might become ambiguous.

The literal-storage choice also avoided deciding which edits were harmless cleanup and which changed the user's intended name. That restraint had an appeal, but it left several text questions outside the simple range check: what counted as a character, how visually identical strings compared, and how invisible spacing affected display.

## Why the record is superseded

The old decision's simplicity was incomplete. A numerical range and literal persistence did not by themselves define a predictable text-entry experience. The later policy handles the current name-length decision.

Name length policy is the replacement authority. The top status link matters because a reader finding this record by its title could otherwise treat the old range as current. The historical value is the reasoning about preserving user intent and avoiding silent truncation, not continued authority over accepted input.

## Connection to existing controls

The current board-code field has a 32-character control limit for a completely different reason: its canonical code syntax is bounded and validated by a parser. The snapshot textarea has its own much larger limit plus a UTF-8 byte check. Those limits should not be generalized from this retired name decision.

Text entry policy, Form layout guide and ADR 042 are useful related pages. They concern the interaction around entering and correcting text, while this record preserves one specific historical validation choice.
# ADR 057: Split the view by behavior

This record explains the component boundaries and the targeted rendering work that keeps large boards responsive.

## Context

A single game component could contain the select, status, 256 buttons, snapshot editor, timers and storage effects. That would be quick to start and difficult to review once input, import and visibility interact. The project instead separates the view by behavior while keeping the composition easy to follow.

`Game.tsx` is the assembly point. `Controls` owns deal actions, `GameStatus` renders progress and completion, `Board` renders and navigates cards, and `Reproduction` owns the disclosure and drafts. Browser session behavior lives behind `useGame`. These boundaries correspond to real responsibilities rather than a generic component taxonomy.

## Small does not mean responsibility-free

`Card` is a leaf button with the state descriptor, face renderer and event callbacks it needs. `Board` calculates face-up and matched membership and supplies positional props. `useBoardFocus` owns remembered focus and navigation. The session controller decides how an activation changes the game and when browser time is synchronized.

This arrangement prevents a card from reading storage or deciding whether a snapshot load should pause. It also prevents the controller from querying every button to paint its revealed state. Each layer can be understood in terms of the data or browser effect it actually owns. React boundaries explains those connections.

## A concrete rendering concern

The active clock can update often, and a 16x16 board contains many buttons. The board memoizes the face-up set from matched positions and selection, and separately memoizes matched membership. It passes a stable activation callback that reads the latest handler through a ref. `Card` is memoized.

A pure clock tick that preserves selection and matched arrays therefore does not force every unchanged card to render again. The optimization follows an observed repeating update. It is not a reason to make every value global or to hide the data flow behind a subscription framework.

## Styles and tests follow the boundary

Card styles sit with `Card`, board layout with `Board`, status styles with `GameStatus`, and control styles with controls. The diagnostic face sheet renders the actual card outside the main controls to verify that its appearance does not depend on unrelated parent styling. That is useful evidence that the component owns its own presentation.

Focused tests sit near the associated behavior, while browser journeys span the assembled application. The source-size specification aims for 100 lines per TypeScript file and limits authored files to 200 lines. The audit checks that ceiling. These constraints keep authored files reviewable.

## Alternatives

A monolithic component would reduce imports but mix unrelated reasons to change. Splitting every few lines into a new component would create indirection without a stable behavior boundary. A generic reusable-control framework could add configuration for cases this game does not have. The chosen middle ground uses small named pieces with concrete jobs.

Props do repeat some data, but that repetition is visible and type checked. A reviewer can trace how a closed card receives `null` instead of a face ID. Hiding that relationship behind an ambient store would make the information boundary harder to inspect.

## Consequences

More files mean more navigation, so direct imports and meaningful ownership matter. The payoff is that a focus bug, parser fix or status-layout change usually has an identifiable home. ADR 001, ADR 016, CSS organization and Source layout are the companion pages. The aim is understandable behavior with targeted rendering work, not file count as an end in itself.

## Stable card inputs in the board

The board keeps membership calculations and callback identity stable across clock-only renders, while the latest controller callback remains reachable.

```tsx
const { size, deck, matched, selection } = game;
  const { viewport, element, focused, focusRemembered, navigate, cardFocused } =
    useBoardFocus(size);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ focusRemembered }), [focusRemembered]);
  // A clock tick keeps both arrays, so the cards' props stay equal and no card renders again.
  const faceUp = useMemo(() => faceUpCards({ matched, selection }), [matched, selection]);
  const matchedCards = useMemo(() => new Set(matched), [matched]);
  // The game passes a new handler on each render. Cards keep one callback that calls the latest.
  const latestActivate = useRef(activate);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    latestActivate.current = activate;
  });
  const activateCard = useCallback((index: number) => latestActivate.current(index), []);
  const style: BoardStyle = { '--grid-size': size };
```
# ADR 058: Give additional stored data a distinct namespace

This record explains the naming rule for new stored data while preserving the existing preferences key.

## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes ADR 011. The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## What remains unchanged in the implementation

`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.

The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. Preferences store and Storage failure policy describe the existing behavior.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions.

A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves.

## Reading the rule accurately

The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.

The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. Persistence envelope, Format versioning guide and ADR 053 explain the surrounding boundaries.

This preserves the useful local-storage model while making the successor to the old naming decision explicit. Historical context remains in the superseded record; current readers can follow its replacement link here without treating the old pattern as the convention for additional data.

## The current preferences key and value shape

These are the existing declarations. The new naming decision preserves this identifier rather than silently changing where the application reads its preferences.

```ts
export const DEFAULT_SIZE = GRID_SIZES[0];
export const PREFERENCES_KEY = 'neon-pairs.preferences.v1';
export const PREFERENCES_VERSION = 1;
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
export interface PreferenceStore {
  getItem(key: string): string | null;
  setItem(key: string, value: string): void;
}
```

docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:3:This record explains the JSON snapshot format, its validation boundary and its relationship to a board code.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:7:Export progress as readable version 1 JSON. The snapshot contains `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. It derives the deck from the code and derives completion from matched positions. There is no second serialized deck, pair total or win flag to reconcile with the underlying data.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:9:JSON was selected because both browser and Node tools can read it, a person can inspect it during a bug report, and copying it from a textarea needs no additional file or clipboard API. The export uses two-space indentation. Formatting makes a report easier to read, while validation relies on values rather than indentation.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:13:`decodeSnapshot` treats parsed data as unknown. It checks the complete shape, version, code, bounded integer counters, matched positions and selection. Extra keys are rejected. Matched positions must be unique, in range and form whole face pairs. A pending mismatch needs two different unmatched positions whose faces differ, with remaining time from 1 through 800 whole milliseconds.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:15:The decoder also checks relationships. Moves must cover the matched pairs and a pending mismatch. An unstarted game has no progress. A started game with zero moves needs its first revealed card. These checks prevent combinations that contradict the current state rules without requiring an exhaustive reconstruction of earlier play. Snapshot selection notes explains the selection cases.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:19:Positions are zero-based row-order indices. Export sorts matched positions so equivalent sets have a stable readable ordering. Active time can retain fractions in memory; export floors elapsed milliseconds and rounds pending mismatch time upward. Rounding the remaining interval upward keeps a still-open mismatch from becoming a zero-duration serialized state.
docs/adr-010-snapshot-json.md:21:The UTF-8 snapshot limit is 65536 bytes. The textarea also has a character limit, but the parser's byte check is the format boundary. This matters because a character count and a UTF-8 byte count are not interchangeable in general. `TextEncoder` supplies the byte measurement in the shared format helper.

docs/adr-030-move-cap.md:15:At the cap, that same code still creates a mismatch or appends a matched pair. There is no branch that returns early merely because the count cannot increase. docs/adr-030-move-cap.md:19:Snapshot decoding accepts nonnegative safe-integer moves through the cap and rejects larger values. It also checks that moves are at least the number needed for recorded pairs and a pending mismatch. A bounded counter alone would not make a snapshot coherent.
docs/adr-030-move-cap.md:21:Saved best counts use the same upper limit. The preference parser also checks each score against the minimum pair count for its size. These checks keep imported and stored values within the same numeric range that the game can display and produce. Replay naturally uses the rule function, so it reaches the same saturation behavior without a separate replay counter implementation.
docs/adr-030-move-cap.md:31:`move-cap.test.ts` and completion tests exercise behavior at the boundary. docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:3:This record explains why an unfinished snapshot waits for Resume before accepting play or active time.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:7:A snapshot can contain one revealed card or a mismatch with only a few milliseconds left. Loading it is an inspection task as well as a continuation task: the player may still be reading the status, checking the board or closing the reproduction panel. Letting the loaded clock run immediately could consume the remaining observation interval before the player was ready.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:9:The decision is to load unfinished progress into a paused session. Resume clears that pause. Completed progress stays completed and has no Resume action. The pause belongs to the session wrapper, not to the serialized selection union, so the same valid snapshot can be interpreted by pure tools without browser UI state.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:13:`replaceGame` computes pause from whether the operation is an import and whether the loaded game is won. It increments generation, resets celebration and updates the selected size. The loaded game itself retains its selection and remaining time. Pausing does not close the mismatch, reset moves or turn a one-card selection into a closed state.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:17:The visible status says “Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.” Completed progress has its separate load status. These messages make the session state explicit rather than requiring the player to infer pause from an unchanging clock. Reproduction panel documents the controls.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:27:Immediate continuation would have been simpler but hostile to snapshots near a mismatch edge. Automatically closing the mismatch on import would have changed the saved progress. Restarting its full interval would have changed remaining active time. A separate modal inspection screen would have added another navigation and dialog problem to a small reproduction workflow.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:29:The inline Resume path makes the pause explicit without turning loading into another game mode. Board codes do not need it because they load a fresh unstarted arrangement. Completed snapshots do not need it because no further active interval remains.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:33:Session tests assert blocked activation and ticks while paused. Browser tests load progress, attempt reveals, move focus, resume and verify the remaining mismatch interval. Completion imports are also checked for a static completed presentation and the absence of Resume. Exact timing tests ensure waiting before Resume contributes no active time.
docs/adr-037-snapshot-pause.md:35:The pause is not serialized back as an extra snapshot field. Export still describes the game progress, while browser continuation is controlled by the session. This keeps format version 1 independent of focus, disclosure state and temporary import workflow. ADR 010, Snapshot selection notes and Clock design explain those boundaries.

docs/adr-042-error-copy.md:7:A board-code or snapshot load is an explicit request to replace a game. Invalid input should explain that the request failed without pretending that the current board was replaced. The player also needs the original draft available to correct. An error that clears the field or resets the game would make validation itself destructive.
docs/adr-042-error-copy.md:9:The decision is short, control-specific feedback. The board loader reports “Invalid board code.” The snapshot loader reports “Invalid snapshot.” The visible notice stays beside the reproduction controls. The current session's game remains intact after a failed parse.
docs/adr-042-error-copy.md:13:`useGame.loadBoard` trims the submitted code, checks it and returns `false` after publishing the invalid-code notice if parsing fails. Only a valid code reaches clock reset and game replacement. `loadSnapshot` follows the same order with `decodeSnapshot`. This order is the behavioral foundation underneath the copy.
docs/adr-042-error-copy.md:19:Snapshot validation checks many relationships: shape, version, code, integer limits, matched pairs and selection consistency. Exposing every parser branch as a separate browser sentence would produce a much larger message surface than the current form needs. The submitted JSON remains available for inspection, and engineering tools can use focused tests and formats to investigate specific cases.
docs/adr-042-error-copy.md:25:The code form's input is keyed by session generation. Invalid input does not change generation, so the edited draft remains. A successful load remounts the input with the current canonical code and focuses the load button. The snapshot draft is local component state and is likewise retained for correction on a failed load.
docs/adr-042-error-copy.md:33:The tradeoff is limited diagnostic detail in the UI. A malformed JSON document and a coherent-looking but inconsistent snapshot receive the same browser message.
docs/adr-042-error-copy.md:35:Browser tests check that invalid drafts leave the current state and selected size intact and that repeated invalid submissions remain separate feedback events. Parser tests cover the underlying malformed inputs. Error message style, Controls and Import safety policy provide the complementary references.

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a memory game that runs offline from one HTML file and keeps local best moves for each board size.

You can repeat a deal with its board code, save progress as a snapshot or run timed actions through the replay command.

Status: implements product spec version 2.2.

## Install

Use the named test combination, Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0 and Playwright 1.64.1 with Chromium 156.0.8078.4. From this folder, install the locked tools:

```powershell
npm ci --cache .npm-cache
```

Chromium 156.0.8078.4 comes with the project's image, so browser tests need no download. Browser tests use fresh contexts. They stop their browser and local HTTP server when they finish.

## Play

Run `npm run build`, then open `dist/index.html` from disk. The game makes no network requests. To keep saved sizes and scores on a stable HTTP origin, run `npm run dev`. Stop it when you finish.

Use Grid size to choose a board. Reveal two cards with a click, tap, Enter or Space. Arrow keys move board focus. Other keys stay with the browser. Tab leaves the board. New Game gives another deal. Restart repeats the current deal.

Open Reproduce a game to load a board code or export progress. Loading an unfinished snapshot pauses it. Resume returns focus to the remembered card and continues the remaining mismatch interval. A completed snapshot loads as completed without Resume. Elapsed time stops at 359999999ms while play continues. The minutes and seconds display reaches 5999:59. Moves stop at 999999. Matching and victory continue at that count. Saved bests use the same move limit.

## Replay

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` with a version 1 replay JSON file. Valid input prints only its final version 1 snapshot JSON to stdout and exits 0. Invalid input prints nothing to stdout, writes a message to stderr and exits nonzero. The command's silent flag suppresses its npm banner so stdout stays JSON. Other npm commands keep their errors and warnings. Replay timestamps can reach the safe integer limit. Elapsed time uses the same cap as browser play.

## Check

Run the checks from this folder:

```powershell
npm run typecheck
npm test
$env:NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION = '1'
npm run test:e2e
npm run format:check
```

`npm test` runs the unit and static checks with Vitest 5.0.5. `test:e2e` type checks and builds current source before opening the new HTML. It also builds the face sheet and session harness as separate diagnostic entries. The game distribution contains no diagnostic entry.

The browser command writes the Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions it ran on to `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. With `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` set to `1`, it also fails unless they match the named combination. Use the flag for named-combination evidence. Other supported runtimes, such as Node 24.19, run without it.

The locked install, type check, Vitest unit tests, build from current source and Chromium journeys have passed on the named combination with the flag set. Other versions have no test record here.

## Accessibility

Keyboard, card names, atomic turn feedback, reduced motion, touch scrolling and the equivalent zoom layout at 640x400 CSS pixels with device scale 2 have browser checks. The diagnostic face sheet draws all 128 faces at 44px.

Playwright checks Chromium's accessibility tree through a complete keyboard journey. It checks controls, card names, states, turn results, the final summary, Tab exit and New Game. The developer provides this tree evidence and the tool record. You confirm spoken output during acceptance with your screen reader.

Tree record: Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1. Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.

Delivered projects from document setups keep the product specification in `docs/`.

Follow the requirements in docs/ for this project.
# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. Pairing covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. Rounds covers event stages. Boards and deals distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. Ties and scores address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

Reproducibility explains the existing technical tools. Competition research describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. Architecture, session module and React boundaries give the broader engineering context.

# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Ada | 1 |
| Second | Bo | 2 |
| Third | Cora | 3 |
| Fourth | Dev | 4 |
| Fifth | Emi | 5 |
| Sixth | Finn | 6 |
| Seventh | Gia | 7 |
| Eighth | Hal | 8 |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

Competition deals covers board identity. Competition ties covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.
