# Neon Pairs 2.2: current release

These release notes describe the current Neon Pairs game at specification version 2.2, covering the work that brought its browser and core behavior into agreement.

The game implements specification version 2.2; the package version is `1.0.0`.

## The release in practical terms

Neon Pairs currently offers seven square board sizes, pointer and keyboard card activation, a remembered board tab stop, local best move counts by size, reproducible board codes, explicit snapshot export and import, and a developer replay command. The distribution is one offline HTML document. There is no account or service required for play.

The smaller release is about edges rather than another menu. A fractional remainder of a miss remains meaningful until it expires. An overdue interval is synchronized before another click. A restored unfinished board waits for Resume. Large boards and the equivalent zoom layout keep their controls readable and their focused card visible. These details make the same rules survive the conditions that a short demonstration rarely reaches.

## Time keeps its precision until export

`performance.now()` supplies the browser's monotonic observations. `elapsedStep` computes positive finite deltas while active, and live game state retains fractions of milliseconds. The 40ms clock interval is a scheduling cadence, not an instruction to add exactly 40ms on each callback.

This distinction matters when the browser is busy. A callback that arrives late can observe the full elapsed delta. A card activation synchronizes the clock first, so a miss that has already expired cannot remain an input barrier simply because its scheduled timer has not run yet. `tests/fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` exercises both a fractional interval and an overdue mismatch followed by a click in the same task.

At the snapshot boundary, elapsed time is rounded down and pending mismatch time is rounded up. A final quarter millisecond therefore exports as one remaining millisecond. This keeps the text format integral without making live state expire early. The clock incident gives a failure analysis around these choices.

Elapsed time is capped at 359999999ms, displayed at the limit as 5999:59. Moves are capped at 999999. Reaching either cap does not end the game or prevent later matches. The elapsed cap also does not stop a pending mismatch's remaining interval from advancing: `advanceGame` clamps the accumulated total while still subtracting the supplied delta from the selection's remaining time.

## Pause and completion have explicit boundaries

The page's hidden interval is excluded from active time. An unfinished snapshot also introduces a pause, with card activation blocked and focus movement available. Resume establishes a fresh clock observation and hands focus back to the remembered board card before its button is removed.

A completed snapshot follows a different route. It appears completed, has no Resume button, and shows a static result. It does not pass through the winning-action record update. Completing unfinished imported progress through actual play can update the local best, because that path reaches `activateSession` with a newly won state.

These distinctions are covered by session unit tests and browser snapshot journeys in the repository. They are also useful when describing a bug. “Loading finished progress” and “finding the last pair after Resume” may produce the same matched positions but have different session effects. The snapshot guide describes the data; session module describes its browser meaning.

## Navigation reaches the visible result of a move

The board still renders all card buttons, including matched ones. Only the remembered position participates in the page's tab order, and ordinary arrows move within row and column bounds. Matched cards have an unavailable action while retaining their place in the geometry.

Focus tests cover entering with Tab and Shift+Tab, returning from Resume, and changing from a pointer click to arrow navigation. Nearest alignment matters especially when the remembered card is far from the current scroll window. The current helper remembers the board's scroll position, restores that basis, and then brings the card into view, counteracting browser centering during native Tab entry.

A visible card is not enough if its outline is clipped. Current card CSS gives a 6px scroll margin, while the shared focus style uses a 3px white outline offset 2px from the target. Browser checks inspect the bounds around first, last, and interior positions rather than treating focus as merely an active-element assertion.

## Zoom and scrolling have concrete evidence

The specification describes the equivalent layout of 200% browser zoom from 1280x800 as a 640x400 CSS-pixel viewport with device scale 2. The game's zoom journey uses that configuration and exercises a completed small board, snapshot loads, and a large board with keyboard movement to the last card.

That evidence is more specific than a general claim that zoom works everywhere. It checks readable controls, status, and summaries without overlap, page width within the viewport, and a focused large-board card inside the scroll area. The game leaves zoom enabled. The zoom behaviour page explains the present layout, and phone research gives the observational context.

The large-board contract also names 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS-pixel views. All 256 positions remain present at the largest size, while overflow belongs to the board. Native controls remain reachable outside that internal scrolling surface.

## What the repository records about tools

The README records a named combination of Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0, Playwright 1.64.1, and Chromium 156.0.8078.4. It says the locked install, type checking, Vitest unit tests, build, and Chromium journeys passed on that combination with the named-combination flag set. Other supported runtimes need their own result records.

The browser command builds current game source and diagnostic entries before starting its Node test runner. The diagnostic face sheet and session harness are separate from the shipped game. A stale `dist` is not the intended fallback if the current build fails. `test-results/browser-runtime.json` is the named runtime record described by the README.

The runtime packages are React and React DOM 19.3.1. The checked-in tool configuration includes TypeScript 7.0.2, Vite 8.3.5, and Vitest 5.0.5. Technology and build pipeline cover their roles.

## Accessibility evidence has a stated limit

The README records an accessibility-tree journey with Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1. It explicitly records that a screen reader was not run. Spoken-output confirmation remains a user acceptance activity.

The journey covers control names, hidden and visible card information, turn results, final moves and time, leaving the board, and starting again. Consecutive identical outcomes are distinct session events; timer renders do not republish them. The screen-reader research page explains how to interpret that evidence alongside the study findings.

Version 2.2 retains version 1 board codes, snapshots, and replays. The current outcome is a small, inspectable game whose behavior is described at the same boundaries the code uses: pure transitions, browser session effects, presentation, and explicit data exchange. Known issues and roadmap notes address unresolved questions without expanding this release's commitments.
# Changelog style

This guide explains how Neon Pairs release notes describe changes in behavior, compatibility and evidence without becoming a second specification.

A release note helps a reader understand what a particular revision changes for play, reproduction or development. It can point to a detailed rule or decision, but its first job is to name a recognizable consequence. The examples below show how release notes describe changes in the game.

## Lead with the changed experience

“Restart repeats the current deal” is more informative than “improved game controls”. It identifies both an action and the result a player can expect. A note about a fix can be more specific still: “Restarting during a mismatch clears the old turn; its pending update cannot close a card in the restarted game.” That sentence gives the trigger, the unwanted interaction and the corrected behavior.

The corresponding implementation is split between game replacement and session timing. `replaceGame` increments `generation`, and `tickSession` ignores an update carrying another generation. A release note can mention that mechanism when engineers need it, but the behavior belongs first. New game and restart supplies the full interaction contract.

An implementation-only note is appropriate when its consequence is a development workflow change. For example, a note about the browser command can say that `npm run test:e2e` builds current source before testing the resulting HTML. The point is which artifact was tested. Merely saying “updated test infrastructure” leaves the reader unable to tell what became more reliable.

## A change statement and its source

These examples show useful release-note granularity through changes in the game.

| Example note | Where its current result is visible |
| --- | --- |
| Matched cards remain available to keyboard focus, with their matched state exposed. | `board/Card.tsx` and board focus behavior. |
| Hidden cards omit their face artwork and identity from the rendered card. | `board/Card.tsx` and `board/card-state.ts`. |
| Invalid board and snapshot loads retain the entered text and active game. | `session/use-game.ts` and the reproduction controls. |
| Export produces readable snapshot JSON in the textarea for manual copying. | `controls/Reproduction.tsx` and `snapshot.ts`. |
| The replay command reports an invalid action's position in its diagnostic. | `scripts/replay-cli.ts`. |

The paths in that table are shorthand within the game source, except the explicit script path. A finished note can name the full path if the implementation detail matters. It does not need to enumerate every file touched by the change. A file list tells someone how a patch was organized; a release note tells them why the patch matters.

## Copy changes have behavioral context

A copy note can quote a short current string. “An unfinished snapshot load reports ‘Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.’” explains why the status includes an instruction. The relevant change is not simply “friendlier text”; it helps a player understand the paused state.

Control names are also concrete references. “Load board” and “Load snapshot” identify different replacement operations. “New Game” and “Restart” identify different deals. A release note that uses “reset” for all four may sound shorter but loses the information a reader needs to follow the change.

## Versions name different artifacts

The specification is at 2.2. Board codes use the `np1` generation prefix. Snapshots and replays have format version 1. The game package identifies itself as `1.0.0`. These numbers are not interchangeable release counters, so a note about one names its subject explicitly.

A useful compatibility sentence for the current specification is: “Specification 2.2 retains version 1 board-code, snapshot and replay formats.” It tells someone with saved reproduction material what to expect. It does not imply that every implementation change is a format migration.

A deck-generation change would be especially consequential because the board-code version fixes the algorithm. A note discussing such a proposal belongs with Board code format and Deck generation; it cannot claim unchanged reproducibility just because the code's visible spelling stayed familiar. Conversely, moving code between modules does not by itself alter a serialized version.

## Evidence is part of the release account

An implementation statement and a verification statement support different conclusions. “The build emits a self-contained `dist/index.html`” describes the distribution design. “The resulting HTML was opened from disk with network access blocked” describes an executed check. The second statement belongs in a release record only when that check was actually performed for the release being described.

The repository README records Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0, Playwright 1.64.1 and Chromium 156.0.8078.4 as the named tested combination. It also says a screen reader was not run. A release note can summarize that bounded evidence and link to Browser support or Accessibility audit. It cannot turn the recorded Chromium result into a claim about every browser or spoken output.

The source tests provide places to look for specific evidence: `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks literal labels and statuses, `tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` checks repeated feedback events, and `scripts/replay.test.ts` checks command output and failures. Mentioning a test file is useful traceability. It is not the same as reporting a passing run.

## A compact note, with commentary

The following corrective-release entry describes recovery behavior:

> Reproduction tools keep invalid drafts available for correction. Loading an unacceptable board code or snapshot reports the relevant notice and leaves the active game in place. The replay command gives file-specific diagnostics on stderr while leaving stdout available for successful snapshot JSON.

The first sentence names the reader benefit. The next two separate browser recovery from command-line output. The paragraph does not need a catalogue of parser branches because those belong in reference documentation. It also avoids implying that a browser notice now diagnoses every individual field.

For a smaller release, the first two sentences could stand alone. For a release centered on replay, the last sentence could lead and point to an example diagnostic. The right length follows the change's consequences. Documentation style covers source-grounded examples, and Release checklist is the place to find the operational checks that accompany publication.
# ADR 055: Review behavior and evidence together

This record explains the rationale for reviewing behavior and evidence before integration.

## Decision context

The project uses small modules, strict typing and several layers of tests, but none of those tools independently decides whether a change expresses the intended game behavior. A parser can be well typed and accept the wrong fields. A timer can be thoroughly tested and still use a mistaken definition of active time. Review connects the stated behavior to the implementation and its evidence.

The workflow discussion favored review before integrating a change so that behavior, implementation and evidence could be assessed together.

## What a reviewer can assess

A useful change description starts with the trigger and resulting behavior. For a mismatch fix, the reviewer needs to know whether the problem occurred at an exact closing edge, after visibility changed or after replacing a deal. Those are different risks even if all involve a timer.

The source then makes the mechanism inspectable. Pure transitions live in `game.ts`; browser observation and lifecycle live in the session hooks; focus and scrolling live in the board. A change that crosses those boundaries deserves an explanation of why each piece moves. Architecture supplies that shared vocabulary.

Evidence follows the claim. A literal deck vector supports generation stability. A parser test supports rejection of an inconsistent snapshot. A browser journey supports the focus result after Resume. A screenshot supports an artwork observation. Review is stronger when the evidence matches the behavior than when a long list of unrelated commands is attached.

## An example review path

Consider changing the clock so a late callback closes a mismatch correctly. The reviewer can inspect whether measured deltas remain fractional, whether the current generation is checked and whether synchronization still happens before activation. Focused clock tests can exercise arithmetic; browser edge tests can show the adapter's effect.

A broad refactor that merely moves code has a different burden: the reviewer looks for preserved boundaries, unchanged format constants and stable imported behavior. A formatting-only change has less semantic surface. Scaling explanation to the actual change keeps the process useful rather than ceremonial.

## Alternatives and costs

Relying solely on a green suite would make untested assumptions easy to integrate. Requiring human review to manually repeat every automated check would waste time and still be less precise at numeric edges. The chosen rationale gives tools the repeatable assertions and people the interpretation, scope and maintainability questions.

Review adds latency, especially when the change is small. Small behavior files and focused descriptions reduce that cost by making the result understandable. The point is not to expand every fix into a design process; it is to keep the relationship between problem, code and proof visible.

## Historical and current evidence

The repository contains source audits, exact-version checks and a README verification record. Those are concrete aids to review.

Code review guide, ADR 052, ADR 053 and ADR 054 are the neighboring pages. The practical outcome is a reviewable implementation with proportionate evidence.

docs/name-length-policy.md:23:In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.
docs/name-length-policy.md:49:There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy.
docs/name-length-policy.md:53:There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:5:Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:71:The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:75:There are no name-specific tests in the repository because no name entry has been implemented. The useful evidence for a future implementation would connect its draft, accepted model and displayed text using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.
docs/competition-deals.md:19:`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.
docs/competition-deals.md:39:`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.
docs/competition-deals.md:41:That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.
docs/competition-deals.md:43:The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.
docs/competition-deals.md:47:`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.
docs/persistence-envelope.md:29:This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.
docs/persistence-envelope.md:31:There is no feature-envelope serializer or decoder in `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Conversely, no current browser code loads feature records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.
docs/persistence-envelope.md:51:There is no migration chain in the preference store. An unsupported discriminator produces the same fallback as a malformed value. No code attempts to guess an older shape, rename its fields or convert a saved sequence into a best map. A migration requires a code change with observable effects.
docs/persistence-envelope.md:57:The domain state is therefore not the same thing as the serialized object. `Preferences` has no `schemaVersion` field. The writer adds it at the boundary. The reader removes that boundary concern by returning a `Preferences` value with known fields. This is why callers can use `preferences.size` without repeatedly checking a schema version in components.
docs/persistence-envelope.md:59:An envelope serves a similar boundary role for its own record collection, but there is no existing generic persistence framework to extend. The source uses direct imports and a two-method store interface. There is no registry, adapter hierarchy or global storage coordinator.
docs/persistence-envelope.md:63:An empty preference score map is valid. It means no supported size has a saved best in that aggregate. The selected size is still meaningful. By contrast, an absent score-map field, an array in its place, or a map with an impossible score invalidates the preference value. Missing storage and invalid storage reach the same fallback state through different branches.
docs/persistence-envelope.md:65:For a feature collection, an empty array describes a collection with no records. Corrupt data policy deals with rejection and replacement; it is the place to examine how a failed read interacts with later saving.
docs/format-versioning-guide.md:49:There is also no automatic snapshot upgrade on page load. Active progress is not read from local storage. The user explicitly supplies a snapshot through the reproduction controls, and the current decoder accepts or rejects it. Preferences and per-size bests belong to a separate storage contract described in Persistence overview.
docs/dialog-policy.md:5:The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.
docs/dialog-policy.md:11:There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.
docs/dialog-policy.md:13:The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. Focus policy covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.
docs/dialog-policy.md:31:The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
docs/dialog-policy.md:37:A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.
docs/dialog-policy.md:39:Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. Clock design and Mismatch interval explain the established clock model.
docs/competition-pairing.md:5:Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.
docs/competition-pairing.md:30:In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.
docs/competition-pairing.md:34:There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.
docs/competition-pairing.md:58:The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.
docs/retention-policy.md:27:The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.
docs/retention-policy.md:31:The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. Storage quota notes discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.
docs/retention-policy.md:35:The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.
docs/retention-policy.md:41:For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.
docs/retention-policy.md:45:The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.
docs/retention-policy.md:47:The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.
docs/competition-rounds.md:9:The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.
docs/competition-rounds.md:19:Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.
docs/competition-rounds.md:25:`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.
docs/competition-rounds.md:31:This source boundary is valuable in review. Someone can demonstrate the round text in a prototype without having changed the underlying game mechanics. Conversely, reusing the existing status component does not supply a round label automatically. The product concept and its rendered location are separate matters.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:26:A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:32:A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in Board code format.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:36:A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. Replay format covers the timeline and diagnostic result.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:44:`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:54:The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:60:Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.
docs/competition-ties.md:23:The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.
docs/competition-ties.md:49:Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.
docs/competition-ties.md:51:Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.
docs/competition-ties.md:55:The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.
docs/competition-ties.md:69:`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.
docs/competition-ties.md:75:A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. Replay format explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.
docs/competition-ties.md:77:For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:5:The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:11:The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.
docs/duplicate-names-policy.md:49:Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.
docs/tables-policy.md:5:There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.
docs/tables-policy.md:17:GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.
docs/tables-policy.md:23:Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.
docs/tables-policy.md:31:There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.
docs/tables-policy.md:37:The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.
docs/tables-policy.md:47:Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.
docs/tables-policy.md:53:There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.
docs/persistence-overview.md:15:Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.
docs/persistence-overview.md:39:Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.
docs/persistence-overview.md:47:The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.
docs/persistence-overview.md:59:Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. Private browsing notes and Storage quota notes separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.
docs/focus-policy.md:9:`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.
docs/focus-policy.md:13:The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. Dialog policy covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a memory game that runs offline from one HTML file and keeps local best moves for each board size.

You can repeat a deal with its board code, save progress as a snapshot or run timed actions through the replay command.

Status: implements product spec version 2.2.

## Install

Use the named test combination, Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0 and Playwright 1.64.1 with Chromium 156.0.8078.4. From this folder, install the locked tools:

```powershell
npm ci --cache .npm-cache
```

Chromium 156.0.8078.4 comes with the project's image, so browser tests need no download. Browser tests use fresh contexts. They stop their browser and local HTTP server when they finish.

## Play

Run `npm run build`, then open `dist/index.html` from disk. The game makes no network requests. To keep saved sizes and scores on a stable HTTP origin, run `npm run dev`. Stop it when you finish.

Use Grid size to choose a board. Reveal two cards with a click, tap, Enter or Space. Arrow keys move board focus. Other keys stay with the browser. Tab leaves the board. New Game gives another deal. Restart repeats the current deal.

Open Reproduce a game to load a board code or export progress. Loading an unfinished snapshot pauses it. Resume returns focus to the remembered card and continues the remaining mismatch interval. A completed snapshot loads as completed without Resume. Elapsed time stops at 359999999ms while play continues. The minutes and seconds display reaches 5999:59. Moves stop at 999999. Matching and victory continue at that count. Saved bests use the same move limit.

## Replay

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` with a version 1 replay JSON file. Valid input prints only its final version 1 snapshot JSON to stdout and exits 0. Invalid input prints nothing to stdout, writes a message to stderr and exits nonzero. The command's silent flag suppresses its npm banner so stdout stays JSON. Other npm commands keep their errors and warnings. Replay timestamps can reach the safe integer limit. Elapsed time uses the same cap as browser play.

## Check

Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

Elapsed time rules, clock design and mismatch interval describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. Replay format explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.

Preferences store and best score records explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.

## Two ordinary paths have side effects

The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.

The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.

Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game.

There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller.

## Where saving actually happens

`useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted.

Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.

The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.

`rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. Persistence overview and React boundaries cover those existing responsibilities.

## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy

The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.

That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.

`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.

## A concrete review example

Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.

The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.

A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen.

The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear.


`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept.

Similarly, `src/game/Game.tsx` is the composition of a solo session. It passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Neither operation establishes which stage a group has reached. Status bar explains the existing statistics, and React boundaries explains the surrounding composition.

The tournament view now renders the event label as `Round: NAME` in `src/game/tournament/TournamentPlay.tsx`. It keeps that context outside `GameStatus`, whose contract remains limited to one ordinary game and its saved best.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. Mismatch interval and new game and restart cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See Preferences store for the exact validation and React effect. Best score records covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see Snapshot format and Reproduction panel.

A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see Snapshot format and Reproduction panel.

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

# Persistence envelope

This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.

The source currently serializes a preference aggregate, not a collection of feature records. Its key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and its discriminator is `schemaVersion: 1`. The existing reader and writer continue to use that preference format; values already stored in browsers require a code migration to change shape.

## The feature value boundary

A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.

This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records.

The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See Format versioning guide and Data exchange policy when following a value across those boundaries.

## The existing aggregate, precisely

The current storage writer does this:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences })
```

`PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}}
```

This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.

There is no feature-envelope serializer or decoder in `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Conversely, no current browser code loads feature records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.

Preferences store documents the complete aggregate reader. Persistence overview explains why active progress is absent from that value.

## What the preference reader actually checks

`readPreferences` starts with `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` as its fallback. It obtains the stored string, passes it through `parseJson`, requires a non-null non-array object, checks the version and selected size, and then checks the score map. A single rejected map entry returns the fallback for the whole preference value.

# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is Reproducibility. This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See Format versioning for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

# Format versioning guide
This page explains which versions Neon Pairs exposes and how to assess compatibility when its exchange behavior changes.

The current product specification is version 2.2. Board generation, snapshots and replays still use their original format versions. A product release and an exchange format answer different questions: the release says which application behavior was delivered; the format says how an artifact is interpreted. The package's `1.0.0` version is another independent value and does not select a decoder.

## The version map today

| Surface | Version marker | Source authority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting deal | `np1` prefix inside the board code | `BOARD_VERSION` in `deck.ts` |
| Progress position | Numeric root `version: 1` | `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` in `snapshot.ts` |
| Action timeline | Numeric root `version: 1` | `REPLAY_VERSION` in `replay.ts` |
| Product behavior | Specification status 2.2 | Existing game specification |

The JSON version does not absorb the board generation version. A snapshot is version 1 and contains a separately parsed board code. A replay has the same layering. Its action semantics and its starting arrangement both matter, but they are represented by different fields.

This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.

## Compatibility follows the reader

An existing snapshot reader accepts exactly seven root fields and three exact selection shapes. An existing replay reader accepts exactly four root fields and two action fields. Adding an optional annotation may look harmless to its writer, but an unchanged reader rejects it. In these formats, an additive field is not automatically a compatible change.

Property order and whitespace are different. Both readers parse JSON before checking key sets, so a reordered object with the same values is accepted. Formatting can still cross the byte limit. An export style change can therefore be semantically neutral for small files and affect acceptance near a size boundary.

Accepted array order depends on the field. A snapshot's matched list is validated by membership and whole-face counts; export sorts it numerically. A replay's action list is chronological data with stable ordering at equal times. Sorting a replay action list to make output look tidy can change its result even if no timestamp changes.

The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in Data exchange policy and Import safety. They are separate from the accepted version 1 wire definitions. Reading a policy page does not make the current decoder accept fields absent from its exact-key lists.
