# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context.
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in Board code format.

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. Snapshot format gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. Replay format covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See Reproduction panel and Focus policy for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has four exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Tournament JSON carries setup or a bracket, results and current game. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay, and a tournament handoff needs Tournament JSON.

The detailed contract is Reproducibility. This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Tournament JSON uses `format: "neon-pairs/tournament"` and numeric `version: 1`. Every new exported JSON object has a `format`, a whole-number `version`, and keys written alphabetically at every level. Existing formats stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See Format versioning for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |

Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. Storage testing guide describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.
# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context.

# Persistence envelope

This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.

The existing preference source serializes an aggregate at `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, with discriminator `schemaVersion: 1`. Tournament mode also uses the feature collection envelope for completed bracket records at `np3:tournaments`; it does not change the existing preference format.

## The feature value boundary

A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.

This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. Tournament storage writes `{ "items": [...], "v": 3 }`; its items are completed tournament records.

The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See Format versioning guide and Data exchange policy when following a value across those boundaries.

## The existing aggregate, precisely

The current storage writer does this:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences })
```

`PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}}
```

This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.

`src/game/tournament/storage.ts` reads and writes the feature envelope for tournament history. `readPreferences` still expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns default preferences. No browser code loads tournament records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.

Preferences store documents the complete aggregate reader. Persistence overview explains why active progress is absent from that value.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

Ordinary solo play uses `neon-pairs.preferences.v1` for the selected board size and lowest completed move counts. It does not contain a saved game. Tournament mode adds a separate `np3:tournaments` collection for completed brackets; active tournament progress stays in page memory unless exported. Reloading therefore creates a fresh solo deal and restores the completed tournament list.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in Rules.

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in Reproducibility. A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in Input.

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in Neon Pairs.
# Control bar

This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session.

The bar is deliberately small: a labeled size selector, New Game and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`, so the actions that replace a deal are available before entering the board. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see Reproduction panel.

## Component boundary

`src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import.

The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed.

The select and buttons are native elements. The two buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in Board keyboard navigation.

## Labels and options

`src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar.

The options come directly from `GRID_SIZES` in `deck.ts`. Their values are the numeric side lengths rendered as native option values, and their text is the side repeated with a lowercase `x`:

| Display | Value | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4x4 | 4 | 16 |
| 6x6 | 6 | 36 |
| 8x8 | 8 | 64 |
| 10x10 | 10 | 100 |
| 12x12 | 12 | 144 |
| 14x14 | 14 | 196 |
| 16x16 | 16 | 256 |

Those are deal sizes, rather than zoom settings. Choosing 16 changes the game to a 16-row, 16-column deck; it does not squeeze the existing sixteen cards into a different arrangement. The larger boards can exceed the available width inside their scroll container. Pointer and touch explains the consequences for reaching cards.

The component itself receives `size: number`, but the session's `newGame` function checks `isValidSize(size)` before making a replacement. That guard is outside the control and also protects callers that do not originate in the native select. The option list is not the only validation boundary.

## Desktop arrangement

`controls.css` uses flex layout with `align-items: end`, `flex-wrap: wrap`, a `12px` gap and a `16px` bottom margin. The size group is another flex row with `align-items: center` and a `12px` gap. The label sits beside its select rather than above it. The outer alignment brings the actions to the same bottom line if control heights differ.

No explicit column count or button width is needed in this layout. Labels and the browser's select affordance contribute to their natural widths. Wrapping is enabled before the phone media query applies, so the bar can also adapt to a constrained content area on a wider window. The maximum content width and page padding come from `game.css`, not the controls stylesheet.

The shared `.control` class comes from `control.css`: `min-height: 44px`, `padding: 8px 12px`, a `1px` neutral border, an `8px` radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. The select and buttons get a pointer cursor. The stylesheet does not replace the select's browser interaction with a drawn menu. Its popup remains the native control's responsibility.

## Phone arrangement

At `max-width: 599px`, `.controls` changes to `align-items: stretch`. The size group occupies the full line with `width: 100%` and `justify-content: space-between`; its label and select move to opposite ends of that row. The direct child buttons each get `flex: 1`, sharing the following row when there is room.

The media query acts on the current DOM hierarchy. Moving a button into an extra wrapper would change the effect of `.controls > button`. A review of such a refactor can compare computed widths and wrapping before deciding that it preserves the arrangement. The apparent simplicity of a wrapper change can hide a layout change on phones.

The breakpoint is not a board-size breakpoint. A 4x4 and a 16x16 game use the same control bar at the same viewport width. The board handles its own width independently. This separation keeps the controls available even when a player has scrolled to the far end of a large board.

## What the actions replace

In `use-game.ts`, `newGame` creates a code using `freshBoardCode(size, current.current.game.seed)`, constructs the new game, resets the clock adapter and commits `replaceGame(...)`. Restart constructs a game from `current.current.game.boardCode` instead. Both begin with a closed selection, no matched positions, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false` because that is what `createGame` returns.

`replaceGame` increments `session.generation`. The Board in `Game.tsx` is keyed by this generation, so it mounts with a fresh remembered tab stop. The BoardCodeForm input is also keyed by generation and receives the current board code as its default value. A reset is therefore observable in several places without each component inventing its own reset event.

The size is saved through the session preferences path. The current size's best record is read independently for the statistics. Choosing a size with no stored record shows `Best: none`; returning to a size with a record displays that size's value. For the exact display boundary, see Status bar and Best score records.

A pending mismatch cannot later alter the replacement deal. Clock reset and generation checks in the session make stale updates harmless. This is why replacing a deal during its short mismatch display is a meaningful controls test, rather than merely checking that the card count changes.

## Focus and continuity

Clicking New Game or Restart leaves focus on the action button. The components do not call `.focus()` on the board after a reset. A user can press the same action again or Tab forward to the new first card. A size change likewise uses the native select interaction rather than an application focus transfer.

Initial page load also does not select a card on the user's behalf. The board's first card is ready as its tab stop, but readiness is separate from current focus. Focus policy describes this distinction and the different treatment needed when Resume removes its own button.

There is no confirmation step in either callback today. Pressing an action replaces the current deal immediately. Do not infer a pending dialog from the text of an action or from the fact that the old game had moves. The separate Dialog policy records the policy for future actions that leave unfinished work.

## A useful review path

The controls checks in `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` inspect the native option values as well as their displayed text. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks the literal labels. `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts` checks the relationship between Restart and the remembered board entry point. Layout coverage includes a narrow `320x640` viewport in `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` and the equivalent zoom layout in `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`.

These checks cover different failures. A label refactor could preserve a screenshot while breaking name-based selection. A wrapper refactor could preserve all labels while changing the mobile row. A session refactor could keep the bar visually identical while allowing an earlier timer to touch a new deal. Reading the component, CSS and callback together makes those differences visible.

For a manual check, choose a nondefault size, reveal a mismatching pair, then use Restart before it closes. The deck repeats and the counters reset. Use New Game at that same size and confirm that its code changes. Tab into the board after each action to observe the reset entry point. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update.
# Target size policy

This page records the control target policy and explains the size constraints already present in the interface styles.

Target size is about the area a person can activate, not the size of a glyph drawn inside it. A card's marker is small, but the native button enclosing the whole card is the target. The same distinction applies to a summary's disclosure marker and the much larger summary row.

## Policy and present coverage

The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.

The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.

This is a control policy, not a claim of complete accessibility conformance. The visuals specification makes the same distinction for its chosen card minimum. Names, keyboard operation, contrast, visible focus and error behavior still have their own evidence. Interface review checklist gathers those areas without turning a size measurement into a blanket result.

## Size sources in the current code

| Element | Source | Existing size behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card button | `board.css`, `card.css` | Grid tracks from 44px to 88px, square aspect ratio |
| Button, select, input, textarea using `.control` | `control.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px |
| Reproduction summary | `reproduction.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 12px 16px |
| Deal action row | `controls.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |
| Reproduction action row | `reproduction.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |

`game.css` applies `box-sizing: border-box` globally. The declared height constraints therefore include padding and border. Looking only at text line height would underestimate the target, while adding padding to the measured border box would overestimate it.

Cards have `width: 100%`, `aspect-ratio: 1`, zero padding and a `2px` border. Their width comes from the grid track. They do not establish their minimum using the SVG's coordinates or intrinsic artwork size. The current artwork can change shape while the card target remains the same square.

## Why large boards scroll

The inner board calculates a minimum content width from side length, `--card-min` and `--card-gap`. On a sixteen-column board that is 794px before viewport padding and border. A phone cannot display that whole width at once while keeping the current card minimum.

The implementation chooses an internal scroll area. Its `overflow: auto` and `max-width: 100%` allow the board to extend inside a bounded viewport. The outer page stays within the window. This is the reason a sixteen-column board does not respond like a shrunken thumbnail of a four-column board.

A target-size review can therefore encounter two valid observations at once: every card has its intended dimensions, and some cards are outside the current visible portion of the board. Reachability is supplied by scrolling and keyboard movement. Pointer and touch explains the touch path to the last card; Board keyboard navigation explains arrow access.

A partially clipped card also has a full underlying button box. Clicking the visible part can activate it, after which the current implementation scrolls it fully into view. That behavior does not mean the clipping itself should be measured as the card's intended dimensions. It is an overflow case with a separate focus and pointer timing concern.

## Phone layout affects widths

At `max-width: 599px`, the deal size group fills the row and uses space-between alignment. New Game and Restart receive `flex: 1`. This gives the actions room without hard-coding two button widths. The text and browser control still contribute their intrinsic size constraints.

The reproduction action rows also wrap, with buttons growing on the phone breakpoint. The Board code input has `flex: 1`, a preferred width of `16ch` and `min-width: 0`. The textarea fills its parent and can resize vertically. These choices keep the text tools within the available width rather than making the outer page horizontally scroll.

A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.

The overall content has `16px` page padding and a maximum width of `1120px`. A viewport width is therefore not the same thing as a control's available row width. Panel padding, gaps and borders consume space too. Reading the size policy as a viewport measurement alone would skip the layout where the target actually lives.

## Visible content versus activation area

A native button may contain text, a shape or multiple SVG pieces. In Card, the face SVG and matched check mark are descendants of one button, and the click callback is attached to that button. Their separate geometry does not produce separate tiny controls.

The neutral back is a `12px` span with a rotated border and `aria-hidden="true"`. It is deliberately smaller than the card. Counting its bounds as the input target would describe the drawing rather than the event-handling element. Similarly, the matched check is a state mark, not a separate action with its own click listener.

Focus outlines sit outside the control border and do not add activation area. Hover border changes likewise do not expand the target. Measurements used to assess the policy concern the actual element box; measurements used to assess focus visibility include outline width and offset. The project already has separate helpers for that distinction in `tests/focus-bounds.ts`.

The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.

## Zoom, density and CSS units

The policy uses CSS pixels. Device pixel ratio affects the mapping to physical pixels, not the DOM geometry reported by `getBoundingClientRect`. A test at device scale 2 can still report a 44px CSS box. Multiplying the bounding-box result by device scale would answer a different question.

The repository's equivalent zoom layout uses a `640x400` viewport with device scale 2. It checks that controls, statistics and the completion summary remain readable and that both small and large boards remain playable. This is useful complementary evidence for a layout that wraps and scrolls rather than simply shrinking every element.

The game does not disable pinch zoom. Card touch handling uses `touch-action: manipulation`, and index.html does not impose a maximum scale. A target remains part of a browser page whose visible scale can change. Zoom behaviour covers the visual contract in more detail.

## Existing evidence and what it establishes

`tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks the default board and control dimensions at `320x640`. It measures `.controls button`, `.controls select` and `.card` boxes and checks minimum width and height. The same file checks large boards at phone and desktop viewports, where the card floor, viewport height and complete focus ring are important.

Those checks establish the existing tested elements at their stated layouts. They do not automatically cover a future control merely because it shares a color or appears next to a tested button. The source selectors and actual bounding box identify the scope of evidence.

For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.

The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. Native controls guide explains that architectural advantage, while Contrast audit and Focus policy cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.
# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

The game has two kinds of control groups: the always-visible deal bar and the text tools inside Reproduce a game. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. Native controls guide explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.

That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that.

The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. Control bar documents those callbacks and what they replace.

## Board-code form: one label, one submission

BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button.

The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container.

The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group.

On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged.

## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface

Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically.

Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value.

The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform.

A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow.

## Shared control styling

`.control` sets minimum height, padding, border, radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. It is imported by both Controls and the reproduction components. The selectors for button and select add a pointer cursor, while the input and textarea selector handles shrinking.

The shared class does not create a universal component with all semantics and validation built in. A select still has native options, an input still has its own maximum length, and a textarea still has multiline editing. Their association, callbacks and error descriptions remain in the JSX.

`game.css` sets global border-box sizing and a system sans-serif font at `16px` with a `24px` line height. Form controls inherit the font instead of taking a separate browser default. The focus outline is shared through `:focus-visible`, so a form layout also needs enough space for that outline to be seen.

## Outcome text is outside the disclosure

The load notice paragraph and Resume are in `.load-status`, following details rather than living inside `.reproduction-body`. The row has a `12px` gap, wraps and reserves at least `56px` of height. The paragraph grows and has `min-width: 0`.

This placement makes a paused-load outcome usable after the disclosure closes. It also means a selector that searches only inside details will not find Resume or the notice. Tests deliberately inspect the adjacent load-status location. Error display guide follows its content and the load buttons' `aria-describedby` relationships.

Turn output is elsewhere, near the board instructions. The layout does not put every changing sentence inside the form body. The distinction is useful when testing a large phone board: result visibility near the board and load feedback near the text tools are separate observations.

## Reflow and review examples

At a narrow width, the page should be read as a vertical flow of labeled groups rather than a fixed matrix of coordinates. The existing wrapped rows and shrinking fields let content determine height. The default board fits the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport.

A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay.

The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework.

Tournament setup uses native, explicitly labelled inputs for Player 1 through Player 8. It has no placeholder or character counter; acceptance is checked when Start tournament is pressed. Text entry policy, Name length policy and Duplicate names policy define the accepted representation and group checks.
# Interface review checklist

This page is a review route through the existing controls, input behavior and related interface policies.

A useful review follows a few populated journeys and checks source at the transitions. An empty board screenshot cannot show preserved drafts, matched-card focus or a stale timer after Restart. The checks below are grounded in the current source and specifications; links identify the separate policies for feature surfaces that do not exist yet.

## Establish what changed

Start with the actual component and its callback. A control can retain its appearance while changing submission, focus or session behavior. A CSS-only change can also alter the hit area or clipping without touching an event handler.

- Identify whether the change affects `Controls`, `Reproduction`, `BoardCodeForm`, `GameStatus`, `Board`, `Card` or the focus hook.
- Follow callbacks into `use-game.ts` and `session.ts` when the change replaces a game, accepts input or publishes feedback.
- Compare element types, ids, label associations, explicit button types and source order as well as class names.
- Check mobile selectors that depend on direct children before accepting a wrapper-only refactor as behaviorally neutral.

Tournament mode adds a name editor, a native leave/load dialog and a bracket result table. The checks below identify their policies and source boundaries alongside the established solo screen.

## Deal controls

Use Control bar and the Controls specification as the reference for these observations.

- Grid size is a labeled native select with the seven supported choices, and its selected value agrees with the current game after either successful load type.
- New Game keeps the current size and creates a fresh deal; Restart repeats the current board code.
- Both actions reset selection, pairs, moves and elapsed time, and leave their action button focused.
- Replacing a game during a mismatch does not let an old timer change the replacement.
- The board's next native entry starts at its first card after a replacement, rather than retaining an index from the old deal.

A code comparison can distinguish New Game from Restart even when the two visible decks happen to share some positions. A move-count comparison alone cannot establish that distinction. For size changes, check both card count and the controlled select value.

The current buttons act immediately. A reviewer should not claim existing confirmation coverage from the presence of a leave policy elsewhere. Dialog policy records that separate feature boundary.

## Text tools and errors

The useful draft is one that differs from the currently displayed code, and the useful game state has some progress. Reproduction panel and Error display guide provide the source trace.

- The native disclosure starts collapsed and is named Reproduce a game.
- Board code and Snapshot JSON retain visible, correctly associated labels and their existing native limits.
- Editing Board code, then playing a card, keeps the edited draft.
- Invalid board-code and snapshot submissions preserve the current game and the entered text, and show their exact existing load outcomes.
- Successful Board code submission refreshes the field from the accepted code and updates the selected size.
- Export fills selectable, readable JSON without replacing or pausing play.

Try Enter from Board code as well as clicking Load board. Success focuses Load board because the input is replaced. Failure from the input keeps editing focus there. A click-origin failure keeps focus on the clicked action. The distinction can be lost in a test that only inspects the final board.

The snapshot textarea is multiline and has its own local state. Enter is not an implicit import action. Its draft is not automatically rewritten on every turn or deal replacement. The visible notice sits outside the disclosure, so closing it does not hide an unfinished import's way to continue.

## Import and Resume

A valid unfinished snapshot and a valid completed snapshot exercise different paths. The current specification gives concrete examples and constraints in Snapshot format.

- Unfinished progress loads paused, including an imported position that has not started its clock yet.
- Card activation is blocked while paused, but focus movement still works.
- Resume focuses the board's remembered card before its own button is removed.
- A pending mismatch continues its remaining active interval after Resume.
- Completed progress loads completed, with static completion output and no Resume button.
- Import is not treated as a newly achieved play completion for best-record updates.

A far remembered card on a large board makes the Resume check meaningful. Scroll the board away from that card before resuming and inspect both focus and nearest visibility. Merely finding any focused button afterward would not establish that the remembered destination survived.

## Board movement and activation

Use Board keyboard navigation, Pointer and touch and Disabled state guide together.

- Tab enters the remembered card and can leave the board again; reverse traversal is native too.
- Plain arrows move one row or column, stop at edges and do not reveal cards.
- Modifier combinations and unlisted keys retain browser behavior.
- Enter, Space, primary click and completed tap reach the shared card action.
- Hover, touch scrolling, pointer cancellation and context-menu interaction do not choose a card.
- Matched cards stay focusable and expose their matched state while activation leaves the turn unchanged.
- Repeated activation of the first revealed card does not add a move.

For a mismatch, attempt a third activation while the pair is visible and move focus elsewhere. The pair stays until its active wait expires; closure does not drag focus back. Hide and show the page during the interval when a lifecycle change is in scope.

Pointer checks include a card partly clipped at the viewport edge. The source intentionally avoids moving a card under a held pointer, then scrolls it after the click. A centered-card click can pass even when that edge behavior regresses.

## Names and accessible content

Inspect actual DOM and browser accessibility exposure. Visual equivalence is insufficient when hidden data or labels are involved.

- Hidden card names expose position and closed state without a face description or hidden face artwork in their DOM.
- Revealed and matched card names include the correct face description and state.
- Face and check SVGs do not introduce extra focus targets or duplicate the button's description.
- Current statistics expose their visible terms and values without alternate labels replacing the numbers.
- Completion makes the final moves and elapsed time available in the persistent summary.

Screen reader notes records the full journey and the distinction between tree evidence and spoken review. The repository README records the browser and tool versions and says no screen reader was run. A review report should describe the evidence it actually has.

When a feature introduces name input, consult Text entry policy, Name length policy and Duplicate names policy. The existing code and JSON text fields do not establish those name checks. For new result content, consult Tables policy.

## Results and repeated events

Announcements policy owns the publication model. In a populated game, inspect the event output while also checking that ordinary rendering stays quiet.

- A first reveal changes the card without publishing a resolved-turn result.
- A match or miss publishes its result once per resolved turn, including consecutive identical misses.
- Focus movement, clock updates and mismatch closure do not repeat the prior result.
- The winning result combines the last match and completion information.
- Repeated invalid loads and repeated successful snapshot loads each publish their load outcome.

The session's `announcement` value and the keyed feedback span explain repeated identical text. A refactor that only compares feedback strings can accidentally remove the event distinction. A refactor that updates the identity on every render can produce the opposite failure.

docs/data-exchange-policy.md:4:The game has four exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Tournament JSON carries setup or a bracket, results and current game. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay, and a tournament handoff needs Tournament JSON.
docs/data-exchange-policy.md:10:The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Tournament JSON uses `format: "neon-pairs/tournament"` and numeric `version: 1`. Every new exported JSON object has a `format`, a whole-number `version`, and keys written alphabetically at every level. Existing formats stay as they are.
